<!-- source: README.md -->

# oprobe

> **oprobe is a profiler for OpenDAL operators.**
> It shows what your `Operator` really does on the wire, names the layer that fixes it, and proves
> the fix before you ship it.

A program has `perf` and flame graphs. An [Apache OpenDAL](https://opendal.apache.org/) operator
has oprobe. It traces every backend request under every operation, stage by stage (queue, connect,
send, time to first byte, body, retry backoff), explains what it finds as **one OpenDAL change**,
and proves that change with an interleaved A/B test on the objective you care about.

[中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) · [Concepts](docs/concepts.md) ·
[op.toml](docs/operator.md) · [CLI](docs/cli.md) · [Reading the profile](docs/reading-the-profile.md) ·
[Embedding](docs/embedding.md) · [App](docs/app.md) · [Install](docs/install.md) ·
[Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md)

## The loop: Profile → Explain → Prove

1. **Profile.** Drive a workload through an operator (`oprobe run s3://bucket/prefix`), or open a
   `.oprobe` file that [`oprobe-trace`](docs/embedding.md) wrote in production.
2. **Explain.** Each finding names a cause, shows the requests that are its evidence, and names the
   one OpenDAL remedy. It gives no numbers: a single run varies no load and cannot size a change.
3. **Prove.** `oprobe prove` runs the current operator and the one with the remedy interleaved
   (A B A B …), sizes the remedy where it has a size, and decides on your objective (goodput by
   default, or p99). The result is a **proven layer diff** you can copy.

## Start in 60 seconds

```bash
# install (macOS / Linux; Windows, packages and cargo: docs/install.md)
curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

oprobe demo                      # profile a misbehaving S3 lab on your laptop: no account needed
oprobe prove last throttling     # A/B-test the remedy of the throttling finding
oprobe                           # the app: runs, profile, operator, compare
```

`oprobe demo` is `oprobe run lab://demo`: a local S3 that throttles above 24 requests in flight and
turns some requests into stragglers. The brief names at most three findings, each with its remedy
as an `op.toml` path, and the next command. `prove` ends with the diff, for example:

```text
proved on goodput: +31 % [+27, +35], p99 −42 %, 0 throttled (4 A/B pairs)
+ ConcurrentLimitLayer::new(24)
~ RetryLayer::new().with_jitter().with_max_times(4)
```

Then point it at your own storage:

```bash
oprobe run s3://my-bucket/oprobe --set options.region=eu-west-1
oprobe run op.toml --preset range-reads           # your operator, a parquet-like workload
oprobe run s3://a/x r2://b/x fs:///nvme/x         # several operators, one workload: a race
```

Writes go under a fresh `oprobe-run-<id>/` prefix and are cleaned up; `--dry-run` prints the plan,
`--read-only` refuses every write, and `--max-requests/--max-bytes/--max-duration` are hard budgets.

## Your operator: `op.toml`

The unit of everything is the OpenDAL `Operator`: a service, a layer stack, and read/write options.
oprobe reads it from a URL, from a file, or from `[operators.NAME]` in its config file.

```toml
url = "s3://bucket/prefix"
[options]                       # OpenDAL service options
region = "eu-west-1"
[layers]                        # each key is one OpenDAL layer; absent = not in the stack
concurrent_limit = { http = 24 }
retry = { max_times = 3, jitter = true }
timeout = { op = "30s", io = "10s" }
[read]
chunk = "8MiB"
concurrent = 4
[http]
version = "auto"                # auto | h1 | h2
```

`--set layers.retry.max_times=5` or `--set read.gap=1MiB` changes one value. The diff between two
operators renders as Rust and as TOML. [The reference →](docs/operator.md)

## Findings and their remedy

| Finding | Cause | Remedy (`op.toml` path) |
|---|---|---|
| `throttling` | 429/503 above an in-flight level | `layers.concurrent_limit.http`, plus `layers.retry.jitter` |
| `rate_limit` | a request-rate ceiling | `layers.concurrent_limit.http` |
| `key_limit` | a hot prefix or key | the key layout (advice, not a layer) |
| `bandwidth_cap` | a bytes-per-second ceiling | `layers.throttle.bandwidth` |
| `tail_stragglers` | a few very slow server responses | `layers.tail_cut` |
| `hung_requests` | requests that never finish | `layers.timeout.io` |
| `small_ranges` | many small range reads | `read.gap` / `read.concurrent` |
| `slow_multipart` | multipart uploads that crawl | `write.chunk` / `write.concurrent` |
| `repeated_reads` | the same bytes read again and again | `layers.cache` (`FoyerLayer`) |
| `cold_connections` | handshakes on the critical path, HTTP version | `http.keep_alive` / `http.version` |
| `client_bound` | your process is the bottleneck | none in storage; reported as such |

`run` names the remedy; only `prove` puts a number on it.

## Profile production: `oprobe-trace`

Add one layer to your own operator and save a profile the workbench opens like any other run:

```rust
let (layer, handle) = oprobe_trace::layer(oprobe_trace::Config::default());
let op = op.layer(layer);
handle.save("prod.oprobe")?;          // later: oprobe show prod.oprobe
```

`oprobe-trace` is an OpenDAL layer plus an instrumented `HttpFetch` (OpenDAL's own reqwest client,
observed). Memory stays bounded, the overhead is benchmarked (budget ≤ 2 µs per operation), and an
`Exporter` hook (with OpenTelemetry metrics behind the `otel` feature) sees every request.
[Embedding →](docs/embedding.md)

## The app

Run `oprobe` with no arguments: a native window when there is a display, the same app in your
terminal otherwise (also over SSH). Four views: **Runs**, **Profile** (verdict, where the time
went, the request waterfall of the slowest operations, timeline, heatmap), **Operator** (your layer
stack beside each remedy: toggle a layer, press *Prove*, watch the A/B pairs stream in, copy the
diff) and **Compare**. It speaks 简体中文 and English. [More →](docs/app.md)

## For scripts and agents

Every command prints one JSON document with `-o json` (stdout carries only the result; progress
goes to stderr), errors carry stable codes and exit codes (0 ok · 1 runtime · 2 usage · 3 prove
refuted · 4 budget · 5 safety · 130 interrupted), and the JSON Schemas are in [`schemas/`](schemas).
Agents: [`skills/oprobe/SKILL.md`](skills/oprobe/SKILL.md) and [llms.txt](llms.txt).

## Install

| Platform | |
|---|---|
| macOS / Linux | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh` (`-s -- --cli` for the CLI without the app) |
| Homebrew | `brew install hxddh/tap/oprobe` (the app bundle: `brew install --cask hxddh/tap/oprobe-app`) |
| Windows | `irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 \| iex`, the `.msi`, Scoop (`scoop bucket add hxddh https://github.com/hxddh/scoop-bucket`, `scoop install oprobe`) or `winget install hxddh.oprobe` |
| Debian / Ubuntu, Fedora / RHEL | `.deb` / `.rpm` from the release page |
| Rust | `cargo install oprobe --locked` (`--no-default-features --features cli` for the CLI only, `--features gui` for native windows on Linux) |

The macOS and Windows packages are **not code-signed**: the first open needs one confirmation
([how](docs/install.md#first-open-of-unsigned-packages)). Every asset has a SHA-256 in `SHA256SUMS`
and a SLSA build provenance attestation; the install scripts check the SHA-256 and, when the GitHub
CLI is logged in, the attestation ([verifying](docs/install.md#verifying-a-download)).

oprobe sends no telemetry and talks only to the storage you point it at. [Privacy →](docs/privacy.md)

<!-- source: docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

Ten minutes from install to a proven change: profile the local lab, explain what it finds, prove
the fix, then do the same on your own storage. No account is needed until the last step.

## 1. Install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
# or: brew install hxddh/tap/oprobe · cargo install oprobe --locked · Windows: docs/install.md
```

## 2. Profile the lab

```bash
oprobe demo
```

`demo` is `oprobe run lab://demo`. The lab is an S3-compatible server inside oprobe on 127.0.0.1:
it throttles (503 SlowDown) above 24 requests in flight and turns some requests into stragglers.
The default workload writes small objects, then reads them back with 32 workers for a few seconds.

The brief that `run` prints has three parts:

- **the verdict**: what bounds this operator on this workload (throttling, the server, the
  network, your client);
- **at most three findings**, each with its cause, its evidence (counts and the requests
  themselves) and its remedy as an `op.toml` path, such as `layers.concurrent_limit.http`;
- **the next command**, usually `oprobe prove last FINDING`.

The run is saved. `oprobe show last` prints the whole profile, `oprobe show last --by stage`
groups the requests by stage, and `oprobe show --list` lists the history.

## 3. Prove the remedy

```bash
oprobe prove last throttling
```

`prove` takes the run's operator (A) and the same operator with the finding's remedy (B). For a
remedy with a size, such as a concurrency limit, it first runs short trials over that one value
and picks the knee of the objective. Then it runs A and B interleaved (A B A B …) until a
sequential test against the noise floor decides, or the budget runs out. The verdict is
`improved`, `worse` (exit 3) or `inconclusive`, on goodput unless you pass `--objective p99`:

```text
proved on goodput: +31 % [+27, +35], p99 −42 %, 0 throttled (4 A/B pairs)
+ ConcurrentLimitLayer::new(24)
~ RetryLayer::new().with_jitter().with_max_times(4)
```

The diff is Rust you can paste into your operator, and the same change as `op.toml`. To prove a
change of your own: `oprobe prove last --with layers.tail_cut=on`.

## 4. Open the app

```bash
oprobe
```

The app shows the same runs in four views: Runs, Profile, Operator and Compare. In the Operator
view you can toggle a layer, press *Prove* and watch the A/B pairs arrive. See [the app](app.md).

## 5. Your storage

oprobe uses the credentials your OpenDAL code would use (`AWS_*`, `~/.aws` profiles,
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, `AZURE_STORAGE_*`), or the options in `op.toml`.

```bash
oprobe run s3://my-bucket/oprobe --dry-run      # the plan: requests, bytes, objects, ETA
oprobe run s3://my-bucket/oprobe --set options.region=eu-west-1
```

Writes go under `s3://my-bucket/oprobe/oprobe-run-<id>/` and are deleted at the end. To touch
nothing, profile existing objects read-only: `--existing data/2026/`. Budgets stop a run hard:
`--max-requests 100000 --max-bytes 10GiB --max-duration 5m`.

Put your real operator in a file and profile it on the workload that looks like yours:

```bash
cat > op.toml <<'EOF'
url = "s3://my-bucket/oprobe"
[options]
region = "eu-west-1"
[layers]
retry = { max_times = 4, jitter = true }
[read]
chunk = "8MiB"
concurrent = 4
EOF
oprobe run op.toml --preset range-reads
```

The four presets are `small-files`, `large-objects`, `range-reads` and `list-stat`
([concepts](concepts.md#workload)). Several operators run one after another on the same workload
and form one comparison: `oprobe run op.toml r2://bucket/x`.

## 6. Production

To profile the traffic your service already sends, add the [`oprobe-trace`](embedding.md) layer
to its operator and open the `.oprobe` file it saves with `oprobe show FILE` or in the app.

Next: [concepts](concepts.md) · [op.toml](operator.md) · [reading the profile](reading-the-profile.md)
· [CLI](cli.md)


<!-- source: docs/concepts.md -->

# Concepts

oprobe has six ideas: the **operator** you profile, the **workload** you drive through it, the
**profile** that comes out, the **findings** in it, each finding's **remedy**, and **prove**, which
turns a remedy into a number.

## Operator

An OpenDAL `Operator` is a service (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, a file system, …), a stack of layers
(retry, timeout, concurrency limit, …) and the options of its reads and writes. That is OpenDAL's
own model, and it is the unit of everything in oprobe.

oprobe reads an operator from:

- a URL: `s3://bucket/prefix`, `gcs://bucket`, `azblob://container`, `fs:///nvme/x`, `memory://`,
  or `lab://SCENARIO` for the built-in lab; the layers are OpenDAL's defaults plus `retry` and
  `timeout`;
- an operator file, `op.toml` (format `oprobe.operator/6`): the URL, service options, layers,
  read/write options and HTTP client settings ([reference](operator.md));
- a name, `[operators.NAME]` in the config file.

`--set PATH=VALUE` changes one value (`--set layers.retry.max_times=5`, `--set read.gap=1MiB`).
The difference between two operators is itself a value: it renders as Rust builder code and as
TOML, and it is what `prove` hands you.

Comparing two operators that differ in a layer is the same thing as comparing two that differ in
service. So `oprobe run s3://a/x r2://b/x fs:///nvme/x` races three backends with no extra
feature.

## Workload

A workload is an OpenDAL access pattern. Four presets cover the common ones:

| Preset | What it does | Default dataset |
|---|---|---|
| `small-files` (default) | whole-object reads (60 %) and writes (30 %), stats (10 %) | 256 × 64 KiB |
| `large-objects` | multipart writes (80 %) and full reads (20 %) | 2 × 32 MiB |
| `range-reads` | parquet-like: a stat, the footer, then vectored column-chunk ranges | 8 × 16 MiB |
| `list-stat` | lists (40 %) and stats (60 %) over a partitioned prefix | 512 × 4 KiB in 16 partitions |

Shape it with `-c/--concurrency`, `-d/--duration`, `--objects`, `--object-size`, `--rate`
(open loop: operations start on a schedule and latency counts from the intended start, so a slow
server cannot hide behind fewer requests), `--seed` and `--existing PREFIX` (read the objects
that are already there, write nothing).

oprobe writes its dataset under a fresh `oprobe-run-<id>/` prefix, warms up, measures, and
deletes the prefix. The guard enforces budgets (`--max-requests`, `--max-bytes`,
`--max-duration`), `--read-only` and `--dry-run`.

## Profile

A profile is what one operator did on one workload, saved as one `.oprobe` file:

- the operator spec and the workload, so the run replays exactly;
- every operation and every backend request under it, stage by stage: **queue** (waiting for a
  connection or a permit), **connect** (DNS, TCP, proxy, TLS on a fresh connection), **send**,
  **TTFB** (the server's time to the first byte), **body** (the transfer), **stall** (the body
  waiting for your code), and **retry backoff** between attempts;
- the aggregates: throughput and goodput, latency percentiles, per API and per stage, connection
  reuse, bytes and amplification, a per-second timeline and a latency heatmap;
- the findings.

Each operation's wall time splits exactly into queue + backend + retry + client, so "network,
server or my code?" has a measured answer. Long runs keep every aggregate exact and sample whole
operations (failed, throttled and slowest ones are always kept), so memory stays bounded.

`.oprobe` files come from `oprobe run` and from [`oprobe-trace`](embedding.md) in production;
`oprobe show FILE` and the app open both. [Reading the profile →](reading-the-profile.md)

## Finding

A finding names a cause and shows its evidence. It is derived from the profile by fitting simple
limit models to the requests in flight over time (an in-flight ceiling where 429/503 start, a
request-rate ceiling, a bandwidth plateau, a hot key) and by reading the stage split (stragglers,
hung I/O, cold connections, small ranges, slow multipart, repeated reads, a busy client).

Every finding has a confidence: **high** only when the model explains most of the effect and
agrees across repeats. Throttling that made operations fail is reported as throttling, never as
an invalid run. The codes and their remedies are in the [README](../README.md#findings-and-their-remedy);
besides those, `errors` reports failures that are not throttling and `invalid_run` a run whose
numbers cannot be trusted (too short, nothing measured).

## Remedy

Each finding names exactly **one** remedy, as an `op.toml` path: `layers.concurrent_limit.http`,
`layers.tail_cut`, `read.gap`, `http.keep_alive`, … A remedy that is not a layer (spreading keys
over prefixes for `key_limit`) is reported as advice, and `client_bound` has no storage remedy.

`run` gives the remedy and **no number**. A single run varies no load, so it cannot say how
large a limit should be or how much it would help; claiming so would be a guess.

## Prove

`oprobe prove RUN [FINDING]` is the only source of numbers:

1. **Choose the change**: the finding's remedy (the top finding by default), or `--with PATH=VALUE`.
2. **Size it**: when the remedy has a size (a limit, a chunk), short trials over that one value
   find the knee of the objective, within `--max-throttle`.
3. **A/B test**: A and B alternate (A B A B …); a sequential test on the objective, against a
   noise floor learned from A/A pairs, stops as soon as it can decide, or at `--budget`.
4. **Decide**: `improved`, `worse` (exit 3) or `inconclusive` on the objective: **goodput**
   (successful operations per second; the default) or **p99**. Intervals are Wilson/beta and stay
   in range; secondary metrics are shown and never decide. Deciding takes at least 3 A/B pairs;
   with fewer, the verdict is `inconclusive`.
5. **Save**: every trial run is saved as a child of the prove run, hidden from `show --list`.

The result is a **proven layer diff**: the objective's change with its interval, the evidence,
and the change as Rust and as TOML. Every result states where it was validated (the lab, MinIO,
your bucket).

## Where oprobe stops

oprobe is not a load generator for benchmarking storage servers (use warp or elbencho), not a
monitoring system (use OpenDAL's metrics and OpenTelemetry layers, or `oprobe-trace`'s
exporter), not a CI regression gate and not a cloud bill estimator.


<!-- source: docs/operator.md -->

# The operator file: `op.toml`

An operator file describes one OpenDAL `Operator`: the service, its layer stack, the options of
its reads and writes, and its HTTP client. Its format is `oprobe.operator/6` (JSON Schema:
[`schemas/operator.json`](../schemas/operator.json)). The same value builds the operator oprobe
measures, is what `--set` changes, and renders the difference between two operators as Rust and
TOML.

```toml
url = "s3://bucket/prefix"          # any OpenDAL scheme oprobe is built with; lab:// too
[options]                            # OpenDAL service options, checked against the service
region = "eu-west-1"
[layers]                             # each key = one OpenDAL layer; absent = its default
concurrent_limit = { http = 24 }                    # ConcurrentLimitLayer
retry = { max_times = 3, jitter = true, min_delay = "50ms", max_delay = "5s" }   # RetryLayer
timeout = { op = "30s", io = "10s" }                # TimeoutLayer
tail_cut = { percentile = 95 }                      # TailCutLayer
throttle = { bandwidth = "100MiB", burst = "16MiB" }  # ThrottleLayer
cache = { memory = "256MiB" }                       # FoyerLayer (in-memory)
[read]
chunk = "8MiB"
concurrent = 4
gap = "64KiB"
[write]
chunk = "8MiB"
concurrent = 4
[http]
version = "auto"          # auto | h1 | h2
keep_alive = true
```

Unknown keys are errors. Sizes are `"64KiB"`, `"8MiB"`, `"1GB"` or a number of bytes; durations
are `"50ms"`, `"10s"`, `"5m"`.

## `url`

The service: `s3://bucket/prefix`, `gcs://bucket/prefix`, `azblob://container/prefix`,
`oss://…`, `cos://…`, `obs://…`, `b2://…`, `webdav://…`, `fs:///path`, `memory://`, or
`lab://SCENARIO` for the built-in lab. Release builds include S3, GCS, Azure Blob, OSS, COS, OBS,
B2 and WebDAV; `cargo install oprobe --features all-services` adds the rest OpenDAL offers to
oprobe (Azure Data Lake, Azure Files, Swift, TOS, WebHDFS, UpYun, HTTP).

## `[options]`

OpenDAL service options, by their OpenDAL names: `region`, `endpoint`, `access_key_id`,
`enable_virtual_host_style`, `account_name`, `credential_path`, … An option the service does not
know is an error that names the closest valid one (`config.unknown_option`). Values may reference
environment variables as `${NAME}`. Credential options are redacted before anything is printed or
saved.

## `[layers]`

Each key is one OpenDAL layer. The defaults are OpenDAL's, plus `retry` and `timeout`, which
OpenDAL recommends:

- a key that is absent keeps its default: **on** for `retry` and `timeout`, **off** for the rest;
- `false` (or `--set layers.NAME=off`) takes the layer out of the stack;
- `true` (or `--set layers.NAME=on`) puts it in with its default parameters;
- a table puts it in with those parameters.

| Key | OpenDAL layer | Fields (default) |
|---|---|---|
| `concurrent_limit` | `ConcurrentLimitLayer` | `http`: HTTP requests in flight (`with_http_concurrent_limit`); `operations`: operations in flight (`ConcurrentLimitLayer::new`; unset: unlimited) |
| `retry` | `RetryLayer` | `max_times` (3), `jitter` (false), `min_delay` ("1s"), `max_delay` ("60s"), `factor` (2.0) |
| `timeout` | `TimeoutLayer` | `op`: one operation ("60s"); `io`: one read or write call ("10s") |
| `tail_cut` | `TailCutLayer` | cancel and re-issue requests slower than `percentile` (95, within 50..99) of the recent latencies × `safety_factor` (1.5, within 1..5), once `min_samples` (32) latencies are recorded within `window` ("60s", at most 120 s); the deadline is clamped to `min_deadline` ("50ms") .. `max_deadline` (unset: the operation timeout `layers.timeout.op`, 60 s without the timeout layer). These defaults are oprobe's, not OpenDAL's (1.3, 200, "500ms", "30s"); generated Rust spells out every value that differs from OpenDAL's, so pasted code behaves as measured |
| `throttle` | `ThrottleLayer` | `bandwidth` ("100MiB" per second), `burst` ("16MiB") |
| `cache` | `FoyerLayer` over an in-memory foyer cache | `memory` ("256MiB") |

## `[read]` and `[write]`

The options of `read_with` / `reader_with` and `writer_with`; unset means OpenDAL's default.

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `read.chunk` | read in chunks of this size |
| `read.concurrent` | chunks fetched at once |
| `read.gap` | merge ranges closer than this into one request |
| `write.chunk` | multipart part size (OpenDAL clamps it to the service's limits; the profile shows the effective value) |
| `write.concurrent` | parts uploaded at once |

## `[http]`

The `HttpFetch` client (OpenDAL's reqwest client).

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `version` | `auto` (OpenDAL's default: HTTP/1.1), `h1` or `h2` |
| `keep_alive` | reuse connections (default true) |
| `proxy` | egress proxy URL; `"none"` (also `--set http.proxy=none`) means no proxy, whatever `HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY` say; unset (`--set http.proxy=unset`): the environment |
| `ca_cert` | an extra PEM CA bundle to trust |
| `insecure` | skip certificate verification (self-signed development endpoints only) |

## `--set`

`--set PATH=VALUE` (repeatable) changes one value of the operator before a run; `prove --with`
takes the same paths. The paths: `url`, `options.KEY`, `layers.NAME` (`on`/`off`),
`layers.NAME.FIELD`, `read.chunk`, `read.concurrent`, `read.gap`, `write.chunk`,
`write.concurrent`, `http.version`, `http.keep_alive`, `http.proxy`, `http.ca_cert`,
`http.insecure`. `none` removes an optional value, except for `http.proxy`, where it means no proxy
(`unset` goes back to the environment's).

```bash
oprobe run op.toml --set layers.concurrent_limit.http=32 --set read.gap=1MiB
oprobe prove last --with layers.retry.jitter=true
```

## The config file

`$OPROBE_CONFIG`, or `<config dir>/oprobe/config.toml` (`~/.config/oprobe/config.toml` on Linux,
`~/Library/Application Support/oprobe/config.toml` on macOS, `%APPDATA%\oprobe\config.toml` on
Windows). It names operators and sets defaults:

```toml
[defaults]
preset = "range-reads"
duration = "30s"

[defaults.budgets]
max_requests = 200000
max_bytes = "20GiB"

[operators.prod]
url = "s3://prod-bucket/oprobe"
[operators.prod.options]
region = "eu-west-1"
[operators.prod.layers]
concurrent_limit = { http = 64 }
```

`oprobe run prod` then profiles that operator. Precedence of every setting: flags, then
`OPROBE_*` environment variables, then `[defaults]`, then the built-in default.

## The diff

`prove` and the app's Operator view show the difference between two operators as Rust builder
code and as TOML:

```text
+ ConcurrentLimitLayer::new(24)
~ RetryLayer::new().with_jitter().with_max_times(4)

[layers]
concurrent_limit = { http = 24 }
retry = { max_times = 4, jitter = true }
```

`+` adds a layer, `~` changes one, `-` removes one.


<!-- source: docs/cli.md -->

# CLI reference

oprobe has four commands and an alias. Without a command it opens [the app](app.md).

```text
oprobe                     # the app (a native window, or the terminal without a display)
oprobe run   OPERATOR…     # profile; several operators = side by side
oprobe demo                # = oprobe run lab://demo
oprobe prove RUN [FINDING] # A/B test → the proven layer diff
oprobe show  [RUN|FILE]    # the profile; --list for history
oprobe lab   [SCENARIO]    # a local S3 with faults
```

`oprobe COMMAND --help` prints the same flags as this page; a test keeps the two in sync.

## Global flags

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-o, --output text\|json` | the result on stdout as text (default) or one JSON document (env `OPROBE_OUTPUT`); logs and progress always go to stderr |
| `--color auto\|always\|never` | colors (default `auto`; `NO_COLOR` is honoured) |
| `-q, --quiet` | no progress or informational messages on stderr |
| `--non-interactive` | never prompt or redraw (implied when stdin or stdout is not a terminal) |
| `-h, --help` | help (`-h` for a summary) |
| `-V, --version` | the version |

## `oprobe run OPERATOR…`

Profile one or more operators on the same workload. Several operators run one after another on
the same workload and form one comparison. Prints the brief: the verdict, at most three findings
with their remedy, and the next command. The run is saved; `-o json` prints the report
(`schemas/report.json`).

`OPERATOR` is a URL (`s3://bucket/prefix`, `lab://demo`, `fs:///tmp/x`, `memory://`), an
operator file ([`op.toml`](operator.md)) or a name from the config file's `[operators.NAME]`.

**Workload** ([concepts](concepts.md#workload))

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--preset NAME` | `small-files` (default), `large-objects`, `range-reads`, `list-stat` |
| `-c, --concurrency N` | concurrent operations |
| `-d, --duration DURATION` | the measurement window (`30s`, `2m`) |
| `--objects N` | dataset objects to generate |
| `--object-size SIZE` | size of each generated object (`16MiB`) |
| `--rate OPS` | open-loop arrival rate (operations per second); latency counts from the intended start |
| `--existing PREFIX` | profile the objects already under `PREFIX`; writes nothing (implies `--read-only`) |
| `--seed N` | seed of the workload's random choices |
| `--set PATH=VALUE` | change one value of the operator or the workload, repeatable (`--set layers.retry.max_times=5`, `--set read.gap=1MiB`, `--set layers.cache=off`; [paths](operator.md#--set)) |

**Safety**

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | print the plan (requests, bytes, objects written and deleted, ETA) and exit |
| `--read-only` | refuse every write and delete (exit 5) |
| `--max-requests N` | stop after this many backend requests (exit 4) |
| `--max-bytes SIZE` | stop after transferring this many bytes, e.g. `10GiB` (exit 4) |
| `--max-duration DURATION` | stop after this much wall time, e.g. `5m` (exit 4) |

A budget that stops a run saves the partial run and cleans up. Budgets cover the whole command:
every operator of the run. `[defaults.budgets]` in the config file sets defaults.

```bash
oprobe run s3://bucket/oprobe
oprobe run op.toml --preset range-reads -c 16 -d 1m
oprobe run s3://a/x r2://b/x --set layers.concurrent_limit.http=32
oprobe run prod --existing data/2026/ --max-requests 50000
```

## `oprobe demo`

`oprobe run lab://demo`, with the same workload and safety flags as `run`. The lab throttles
above 24 requests in flight and turns some requests into stragglers.

## `oprobe prove RUN [FINDING]`

A/B-test a change of a run's operator. The change is the remedy of `FINDING` (default: the top
finding), or `--with`. When the remedy has a size, short trials pick it first. Then the current
operator and the changed one run interleaved until a sequential test decides on the objective, or
the budget ends. Prints the proven layer diff (Rust and TOML) with its evidence; `-o json` prints
the prove result (`schemas/prove.json`). Exit 3 when the change is worse on the objective.

A verdict other than `inconclusive` needs at least **3 A/B pairs**: when the budget allows fewer,
the verdict is `inconclusive` (exit 0) with a note. The objective's interval uses Student's t for
the number of pairs, and a noise floor learned from a single A/A difference is doubled.

When a budget (`--max-requests`, `--max-bytes`, `--max-duration`) stops the prove part-way, it
still prints and saves the partial result (`budget_exceeded: true`, usually `inconclusive`) and
exits 4; its trials stay attached, so `oprobe show --rm PROVE` removes them.

`RUN` is a run id, an id prefix, `last`, `last~N` or a label. `FINDING` is a finding code
(`throttling`, `tail_stragglers`, …).

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--with PATH=VALUE` | the change to prove instead of the finding's remedy, repeatable |
| `--objective goodput\|p99` | what the change is judged on: successful operations (or bytes) per second (default), or the worst per-operation p99 latency |
| `--max-throttle RATIO` | share of throttled requests a change may cause, e.g. `0.1%` or `0.001` |
| `--budget DURATION` | wall-time budget of the whole proof, e.g. `5m` |

Every trial run is saved as a child of the prove run and hidden from `show --list`.

```bash
oprobe prove last throttling
oprobe prove last --with layers.tail_cut=on --objective p99
oprobe prove 20261122-0915 small_ranges --budget 10m
```

## `oprobe show [RUN|FILE]`

Print a profile: a stored run, or a file (`.oprobe` from `run` or from
[`oprobe-trace`](embedding.md), or a report `.json`). Without an argument, the last run.
`-o json` prints the report (`schemas/report.json`); `--list -o json` the run list
(`schemas/run-list.json`).

A trace from `oprobe-trace` is recognised by its content, whatever its name. Its report has
`run.source = "trace"` and shows `production trace` where a run shows its workload. Each
request counts as one operation, and only the findings that requests support are derived:
errors, throttling, hung requests, stragglers and cold connections. `prove` refuses a trace
(exit 2): it needs a run oprobe drove.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--list` | list the stored runs (prove trials hidden) |
| `--all` | with `--list`: include the prove trials |
| `--rm RUN…` | delete stored runs |
| `--detail` | every section of the profile |
| `--by stage\|api\|conn` | group the requests by stage, storage API or connection |

```bash
oprobe show --list
oprobe show last --by stage
oprobe show prod.oprobe --detail
oprobe show --rm last~3 last~4
```

## `oprobe lab [SCENARIO]`

Serve a local S3-compatible lab with faults until Ctrl-C and print its endpoint. Point any S3
client at it, or use `lab://SCENARIO` as an operator to start one inside a run.

Scenarios: `clean`, `demo`, `throttle`, `stragglers`, `lossy`, `flaky`, `parquet`, `ratelimit`,
`hotkey`, `bandwidth`, `queueing`, `timevarying`, `noisy`.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--bind ADDR` | the address to listen on (default `127.0.0.1:9000`) |

## Run references

`last` (the newest run), `last~N` (N runs before it), a full id (`20261122-091512-ab12`), an
unambiguous id prefix, or a label. `show` also takes a path to a file.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | ok |
| 1 | runtime failure (auth, network, storage, internal) |
| 2 | usage or configuration error |
| 3 | `prove` refuted the change (worse on the objective) |
| 4 | a budget stopped the command |
| 5 | a safety rail refused the command |
| 130 | interrupted (Ctrl-C) |

Errors carry a stable code (`-o json`: `{"type":"error","error":{"code":…}}`, schema
`schemas/error.json`); [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#error-codes) lists them.

## Environment

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OPROBE_OUTPUT` | default `-o` |
| `OPROBE_CONFIG` | the config file |
| `OPROBE_DATA_DIR` | where runs are stored (default `<data dir>/oprobe/`) |
| `NO_COLOR` | no colors |
| `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` | the egress proxy, unless `http.proxy` is set |


<!-- source: docs/reading-the-profile.md -->

# Reading the profile

A profile comes in three shapes:

| | Command | For |
|---|---|---|
| The brief | `oprobe run …` (default output) | the answer: the verdict, at most three findings, the next command |
| The profile | `oprobe show [RUN\|FILE] [--detail] [--by stage\|api\|conn]` | the terminal, logs, issues |
| JSON | `-o json` on any command | scripts and agents ([`schemas/report.json`](../schemas/report.json)) |

The app's Profile view shows the same sections with charts ([app](app.md)).

## The brief

```text
ATTENTION  throttling-bound: 3.6 % of requests were answered 429/503
  throttling       626 throttled responses above 24 requests in flight (high confidence)
                   remedy: layers.concurrent_limit.http, plus layers.retry.jitter
  tail_stragglers  1 in 40 GetObject responses waits > 200 ms for its first byte
                   remedy: layers.tail_cut
  2114 ops/s · 119 MiB/s · p50 5.0 ms · p99 257 ms
next: oprobe prove last throttling
```

(Illustrative: the exact wording follows the version you run.)

- **The badge** is the verdict level: **HEALTHY**, **REVIEW** (worth a look: informational
  findings, a partial run), **ATTENTION** (warning findings), **CRITICAL** (critical findings).
- **The headline** says what bounds the operator on this workload: throttling, the server's
  latency, the network (connect, upload, download), queueing in the client, or the client itself.
- **Findings**: at most three, most severe first. Each has its code, the evidence in one line,
  its confidence, and the remedy as an `op.toml` path, with no number: only `prove` sizes a
  change.
- **Key numbers**: goodput (successful operations per second), throughput, latency percentiles.
- **Next**: the command that proves the top remedy.

## The profile

`oprobe show` prints these sections (`--detail` adds every column, the per-second timeline,
the configuration and the five slowest operations):

| Section | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| header | run id and label, operator, workload, window, concurrency, start time |
| verdict | the badge and where the time went, in one sentence |
| key numbers | goodput and throughput, latency p50/p99/p99.9/max, failed operations, throttled responses |
| findings | every finding: code, cause, evidence, confidence, remedy |
| where the time goes | each operation's wall time split into stages (below) |
| operations | per workload verb: count, ops/s, p50, p99, max, requests per operation, errors |
| backend requests | per storage API (`GetObject`, `PutObject`, …): count, share on warm connections, mean TTFB and transfer, p99, status codes |
| connections | HTTP version, TLS, new connections, reuse, peak in-flight requests, dial time per phase |
| bytes | logical vs backend bytes, read amplification, over-read, requests per operation, cache hits |
| slowest operation | the worst operation request by request (a waterfall), with its async call stack |
| self | the profiler's own health: scheduling lag, CPU, whether the client was saturated |
| cleanup | test data removed (verified), or what is left |

`--by stage` sums the requests' time per stage, `--by api` per storage API, `--by conn` per
connection (cold and warm, per remote address).

### Where the time goes

Each operation's wall time is split exactly; an instant counts once even when requests overlap:

| Stage | Time when … | If it dominates |
|---|---|---|
| queue | requests wait for a connection or an in-flight permit | a concurrency limit or a small pool; see `cold_connections` and `throttling` |
| connect | DNS, TCP, proxy and TLS of a new connection | connections are not reused, or the proxy or TLS is slow (`http.keep_alive`, `http.version`) |
| send | the request body goes out | upload bandwidth; `write.chunk`, `write.concurrent` |
| TTFB | waiting for the first byte (the server's work plus one round trip) | the store or the distance to it; stragglers show as a long tail (`layers.tail_cut`) |
| body | the response body arrives | download bandwidth per stream × streams; `read.chunk`, `read.concurrent` |
| stall | the body waits for your code to read it | the consumer, not storage |
| retry | the retry layer sleeps before the next attempt | throttling or errors; see the findings |
| client | everything else: OpenDAL, signing, checksums | CPU (`client_bound`), tiny objects |

### How it is measured

- **Requests** are observed inside OpenDAL's own HTTP client (reqwest with rustls, exactly as
  OpenDAL builds it): a timed resolver, a connector layer that times each dial, the TLS
  ClientHello timestamp (which splits TCP from TLS), the response's connection identity (cold or
  warm), and the body timed as it arrives and as your code consumes it. Waiting inside reqwest's
  pool for an idle connection is part of TTFB. Kernel TCP statistics (RTT, retransmits) are read
  at the end of a request on Linux and macOS.
- **Operations** are the workload's logical calls (`read`, `write`, `stat`, `list`, a parquet
  scan); every request is attributed to the operation that caused it, including requests in
  OpenDAL's background tasks.
- **Open loop** (`--rate`): latency counts from the intended start, and arrivals that never
  started count in every percentile as censored values, so a slow server cannot hide behind fewer
  requests.
- **Percentiles** are exact when every operation was kept, otherwise from histograms with three
  significant digits. Counts always agree with the totals.
- **The profiler's cost** is measured: `cargo bench -p oprobe-trace --bench overhead` compares
  the same operations with and without the layer (budget 2 µs per operation), and the profile's
  `self` section reports scheduling lag and CPU during the run. A run where the client was
  saturated says so, and its verdict is `client_bound` rather than a server limit.

## JSON

`-o json` prints one document on stdout. `run` and `show` print the report
(`"schema": "oprobe.report/6"`), `prove` the prove result, `show --list` the run list. Numeric
fields carry their unit in the name (`_ms`, `_bytes`, `_ratio`, `_count`), enums are
`snake_case`, and fields are only ever added within 6.x. Errors are
`{"type":"error","error":{"code","message","hint","retryable","docs"}}`.

## Files

A stored run lives in `<data dir>/oprobe/runs/` as one `.oprobe` file (format `oprobe.run/6`: a
zstd stream of the header with the operator spec and workload, columnar segments of operation and
request rows, the per-second timeline, and the report). `oprobe-trace` writes `oprobe.trace/6`
files (one JSON document: the aggregates and the sampled rows). `oprobe show FILE` and the app
open both. 5.x run files are not read.


<!-- source: docs/embedding.md -->

# Profiling production: `oprobe-trace`

[`oprobe-trace`](https://crates.io/crates/oprobe-trace) is oprobe's instrumentation as one
OpenDAL layer. Add it to the operator your service already uses, and every backend request is
timed by stage and aggregated in bounded memory. Save a `.oprobe` file and open it with
`oprobe show FILE` or in the app, like any run.

It is the only crate oprobe publishes with a semver promise. (`oprobe-core` is on crates.io only
so that `cargo install oprobe` works; it is internal.)

## Three lines

```toml
[dependencies]
oprobe-trace = "6"
```

```rust
let (layer, handle) = oprobe_trace::layer(oprobe_trace::Config::default());
let op = op.layer(layer);
handle.save("prod.oprobe")?;          // then: oprobe show prod.oprobe
```

Apply it first, before your other layers (`Operator::new(builder)?.layer(trace).layer(RetryLayer::new())`):
it installs the instrumented `HttpFetch`, and the layers above it then wrap it, so every retry
is recorded as its own request.

## What you get

- **`handle.snapshot()`**: a `Snapshot` with the aggregates so far: per storage API and stage
  (queue, connect, send, TTFB, body, stall; count, mean, p50/p90/p99/p99.9/max), per verb,
  connection reuse and dial times, retries and status codes, bytes, a per-second timeline.
  Aggregates are exact.
- **`handle.save(path)`**: a `.oprobe` profile: the snapshot plus a sample of whole requests
  (failed, throttled and slowest requests are always kept, within `Config::max_rows`). The rows
  saved are moved out of memory, so periodic saves hold the requests of each period; the
  aggregates are cumulative. `snapshot.save(path)` writes the aggregates alone.
- **`Exporter`**: called for every request as it completes, on the request path (keep it cheap).

```rust
struct Slow;
impl oprobe_trace::Exporter for Slow {
    fn on_request(&self, r: &oprobe_trace::RequestRecord) {
        if r.timing.ttfb_us > 500_000 {
            eprintln!("slow {} {} ttfb {} ms", r.method, r.api.label(), r.timing.ttfb_us / 1000);
        }
    }
}
let cfg = oprobe_trace::Config::default().exporter(std::sync::Arc::new(Slow));
```

- **OpenTelemetry** (feature `otel`): `oprobe_trace::otel::config(&meter)` records
  `http.client.request.duration` (seconds) once per stage, with the attributes `oprobe.stage`
  (`total`, `queue`, `connect`, `send`, `ttfb`, `body`, `stall`), `oprobe.api`,
  `http.request.method` and `http.response.status_code`.

## Configuration

`Config` is a builder; every setting has the default OpenDAL's own client has:

| Method | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `max_rows(n)` | 10 000 | request rows kept in memory (aggregates are exact regardless; 0 keeps aggregates only) |
| `http_version(v)` | `HttpVersion::Auto` | `Auto` (HTTP/1.1, as OpenDAL), `H1` or `H2` |
| `keep_alive(on)` | true | reuse connections |
| `max_inflight(n)` | unlimited | cap concurrent HTTP requests; waiting shows as `queue` |
| `extra_ca_pem(pem)` | none | trust an extra PEM bundle besides the system and WebPKI roots |
| `insecure_skip_verify(on)` | false | skip certificate verification (development only) |
| `proxy(Some(url) \| None)` | the environment | an explicit `http://` proxy, or none |
| `https(on)` | true | selects `HTTPS_PROXY` over `HTTP_PROXY` |
| `tcp_info(on)` | true | read kernel TCP statistics at the end of each request (Linux, macOS) |
| `exporter(e)` | none | your `Exporter` |

`handle.transport_error()` says why HTTP requests are not instrumented, if the transport could not
be built (an invalid proxy URL, a CA bundle that does not parse). The operator keeps working; only
in-process services (`memory`, `fs`) are observed then.

## How it works

For HTTP services the layer replaces the operator's `HttpFetch` with OpenDAL's own reqwest client
(rustls with aws-lc-rs, the same pool defaults: no connect timeout, unlimited idle connections per
host, 90 s idle timeout), observed through reqwest's public extension points: a timed DNS resolver,
a connector layer that times each dial, a TLS session store that timestamps the ClientHello, and a
body wrapper that times the transfer and your code's consumption. Nothing is decrypted or
proxied. For `memory` and `fs` it records one request per backend call.

Without oprobe's workload driving it, requests are not grouped into operations: a profile from
`oprobe-trace` has requests and their aggregates. `oprobe show FILE` marks its report
`run.source = "trace"` and shows `production trace` instead of a workload. Each request counts
as one operation there. The findings that requests support are derived: `errors`, `throttling`
(and `rate_limit`, `key_limit`), `hung_requests`, `tail_stragglers` and `cold_connections`.
The ones that need operations or a load oprobe varied are not: `small_ranges`,
`slow_multipart`, `repeated_reads`, `bandwidth_cap` and `client_bound`. A trace has no workload
to replay, so `oprobe prove` refuses it. Reproduce the traffic with `oprobe run OPERATOR` and
prove that run.

## Overhead

```bash
cargo bench -p oprobe-trace --bench overhead              # ~10 s
cargo bench -p oprobe-trace --bench overhead -- --quick   # ~1 s, runs in CI
```

The bench runs the same operations on a plain `memory://` operator and on a traced one,
interleaved, and reports the median difference per operation. The budget is **2 µs per
operation**; the bench fails above it. On a 4-core Linux VM:

```text
oprobe-trace overhead on memory:// (31 rounds × 50000 ops)
  plain OpenDAL         0.798 µs/op
  with oprobe-trace     1.190 µs/op
  overhead              0.379 µs/op  (p10 0.295, p90 0.578; budget 2 µs)
```

`memory://` is the worst case: its backend call costs well under a microsecond, so the difference
is all bookkeeping. Against object storage, where a request takes milliseconds, the layer is lost
in the noise.

## Stability

Within 6.x the API documented on docs.rs, the `oprobe.trace/6` file format and the meaning of
every field are stable: changes are additive. Public structs and enums are `#[non_exhaustive]`,
so read fields freely but build `Config` with its methods. The `__internal` feature exists for the
oprobe binary and has no semver promise; do not enable it.

## The file

`oprobe.trace/6` is one JSON document, readable without oprobe:

```text
{ "format": "oprobe.trace/6", "oprobe_trace_version": "6.0.0", "created_at": "…",
  "service": { "scheme": "s3", "name": "my-bucket", "root": "/data/" },
  "snapshot": { … }, "rows": { "ops": [], "reqs": [ … ], "info": { … }, "sampling": { … } } }
```

`service` is the OpenDAL service the layer was applied to: its scheme, name (the bucket or
container) and root, with no options. A bare `snapshot.save` has neither `service` nor `rows`.

Object keys, request IDs and remote addresses can be in it; credentials never are. Treat a
profile like a log file before you paste it into an issue.


<!-- source: docs/app.md -->

# The app

`oprobe` with no command opens the app, built on [Native Shell (nsh)](https://github.com/longbridge/nsh):
a native window when there is a display, the same app in the terminal otherwise (also over SSH).

```bash
oprobe          # the app
```

| Where | Drawn with | Comes with |
|---|---|---|
| macOS 14+ | AppKit, Core Animation, CoreText | the `.pkg`, the `.dmg` (`oprobe.app`), the macOS archives, Homebrew |
| Windows 10 1809+ | Win32, Direct2D, DirectWrite | the `.msi` (Start menu entry), the Windows archives, Scoop, winget |
| Linux (GTK 4.14+) | GTK 4, Pango | `oprobe-desktop-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz`, or `cargo install oprobe --features gui` |
| any terminal | the nsh terminal backend | every build except the CLI-only archives |

Linux packages for servers (`.deb`, `.rpm`, the static musl archives) have the app in the
terminal and need no GTK. The CLI-only archives (`oprobe-cli-…`, `install.sh --cli`) have no app
at all.

The app has no logic of its own: it calls the same service layer as the CLI (`run`, `prove`,
`show`), so a run started in the app is a run in `oprobe show --list`, and the reverse.

## Four views

**Runs.** The history, newest first, with live runs streaming in (from the app, the CLI or
another window). Each row shows the operator, workload, verdict, goodput and p99. Prove trials are
folded under their prove run. Start a run from here: an operator (URL, file or configured name)
and a preset.

**Profile.** One run: the verdict, where the time went (the stage split of every operation), the
request waterfall of the slowest operations (each request on a shared time axis, coloured by
stage, with its connection, status and request ID), the per-second timeline and the latency
heatmap (horizontal bands above the bulk are stragglers, vertical stripes are stalls). The
findings sit beside the charts with their evidence; selecting one highlights its requests.

**Operator.** The run's layer stack beside each finding's remedy. Toggle a layer or change a value
(a limit, a chunk size), then press **Prove**: the A/B pairs stream in live with the running
estimate and its interval until the sequential test decides. **Copy** puts the winning diff (Rust
or TOML) on the clipboard.

**Compare.** Two runs, or the operators of one multi-operator run, side by side: goodput, latency
percentiles, the stage split and the findings of each.

## Language

The app speaks **简体中文** and **English**. It follows the system locale (a `zh` locale selects
Chinese) and a setting in the app overrides it. The CLI, the JSON output and the run files are
English only.

## Keys

Everything works from the keyboard, in the terminal and in a window; the app's help lists the
keys. In a window the mouse and the platform's usual shortcuts work too.

## Without a display

Over SSH or in a container the app opens in the terminal. Where neither works (no terminal, a
pipe), use the CLI: `oprobe run`, `oprobe show`, `oprobe prove` print the same profile as text or
JSON.


<!-- source: docs/install.md -->

# Installing oprobe

## Quick

| Platform | Command |
|---|---|
| macOS, Linux | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh` |
| macOS, Linux (CLI only) | `curl -fsSL https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.sh \| sh -s -- --cli` |
| Homebrew | `brew install hxddh/tap/oprobe` (the app bundle: `brew install --cask hxddh/tap/oprobe-app`) |
| Windows | `irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 \| iex`, or the `.msi` |
| Windows, Scoop | `scoop bucket add hxddh https://github.com/hxddh/scoop-bucket` then `scoop install oprobe` |
| Windows, winget | `winget install hxddh.oprobe`, once the package is accepted into winget-pkgs ([below](#windows)) |
| Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL | the `.deb` / `.rpm` from the release page |
| Rust ≥ 1.97 | `cargo install oprobe --locked` |

Then try it with no account: `oprobe demo` ([getting started](getting-started.md)).

## The app and the CLI-only build

Every platform has two builds of the same program:

- **the app build** (the default everywhere): the four commands plus the app, in a native window
  on macOS and Windows and in the terminal everywhere ([app](app.md));
- **the CLI-only build** (`oprobe-cli-<ver>-<target>` archives, `install.sh --cli`,
  `install.ps1 -Cli`, `cargo install oprobe --no-default-features --features cli`): the four
  commands, text and JSON, no app. It is smaller and pulls in no UI toolkit, for servers, CI and
  containers.

Both include the common cloud services (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, OSS, COS, OBS, B2, WebDAV) plus
`fs`, `memory` and the lab. `--features all-services` adds the rest.

## The install scripts

`install.sh` (Linux, macOS) and `install.ps1` (Windows) download the archive for your platform,
verify it against `SHA256SUMS`, verify its build provenance when they can
([verifying](#verifying-a-download)) and install `oprobe` (Linux and macOS: `~/.local/bin`;
Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\oprobe`). `sh install.sh --help` and
`Get-Help ./install.ps1` print every option.

| Option | Variable | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `--cli` / `-Cli` | `OPROBE_FLAVOR=cli` | install the CLI-only build |
| `--version X.Y.Z` / `-Version` | `OPROBE_VERSION` | install this version instead of the latest |
| `--dir DIR` / `-InstallDir` | `OPROBE_INSTALL_DIR` | install somewhere else |
| `--no-modify-path` | `OPROBE_MODIFY_PATH=0` | never touch `PATH` (`=1`: add it without asking) |
| | `OPROBE_RELEASE_BASE=URL` | release download base (mirrors, tests; default `https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases`) |
| | `OPROBE_VERIFY=auto\|require\|checksum` | after the checksum: verify the provenance when this machine can (default), insist on it, or skip it |

They find the latest version without the rate-limited GitHub API when they can: the release's
`latest.json`, then the `releases/latest` redirect, then the API.

**PATH.** When the install directory is not on `PATH`, `install.sh` offers to append it to your
shell's rc file (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc` or `~/.bash_profile` on macOS,
`~/.config/fish/config.fish`, else `~/.profile`). Piped from `curl`, it asks on the terminal when
there is one; without a terminal (CI, `docker build`) it changes nothing and prints the line to
add. `install.ps1` adds its directory to the user `PATH` and to the current session. It installs
the native ARM64 build on ARM64 Windows.

**Updating.** Run the install script again, or use your package manager (`brew upgrade oprobe`,
`scoop update oprobe`, `winget upgrade hxddh.oprobe`, `cargo install oprobe --locked`).

## Release assets

| Asset | Platform |
|---|---|
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz` / `aarch64-…-musl` | Linux, static (any distribution); the app in the terminal |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` / `aarch64-…-gnu` | Linux, glibc ≥ 2.35 |
| `oprobe_<ver>-1_amd64.deb` / `_arm64.deb` | Debian, Ubuntu |
| `oprobe-<ver>-1.x86_64.rpm` / `.aarch64.rpm` | Fedora, RHEL, SUSE |
| `oprobe-desktop-<ver>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` | Linux with the window (GTK 4.14+; `install.sh`, `.desktop` entry, icon) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-universal-apple-darwin.tar.gz` | macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` / `x86_64-apple-darwin` | macOS, one architecture |
| `oprobe-<ver>-macos-universal.pkg` | macOS installer: `/usr/local/bin/oprobe` |
| `oprobe-<ver>-macos-universal.dmg` | macOS app: `oprobe.app` (the same binary as the `.pkg`) |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x64.msi` / `-arm64.msi` | Windows installer: `PATH`, Start menu entry, removable in *Apps* |
| `oprobe-<ver>-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip` / `aarch64-…` | Windows portable |
| `oprobe-cli-<ver>-<target>.tar.gz` / `.zip` | the CLI-only build for each target above (`universal-apple-darwin` on macOS) |
| `oprobe.rb` / `oprobe-app.rb` | Homebrew formula `oprobe` and cask `oprobe-app` |
| `oprobe.json` | Scoop manifest |
| `winget-manifests.zip` | winget manifests for the `.msi` |
| `latest.json` | machine-readable index: version, every asset's URL, size and SHA-256 |
| `install.sh` / `install.ps1` | the install scripts |
| `SHA256SUMS` | checksums of every asset |

Archives contain `oprobe` (`oprobe.exe`), `README.md`, `LICENSE` and `CHANGELOG.md`.

## Homebrew

```bash
brew install hxddh/tap/oprobe               # the command line with the app in the terminal
brew install --cask hxddh/tap/oprobe-app    # oprobe.app, the native window (macOS)
```

The formula and the cask have different names, so both can be installed. Each release also
attaches them (`oprobe.rb`, `oprobe-app.rb`) for a local tap.

## Windows

```powershell
irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex   # no admin rights
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe/releases/latest/download/install.ps1))) -Cli
scoop bucket add hxddh https://github.com/hxddh/scoop-bucket; scoop install oprobe
```

The `.msi` installs for all users (Start menu entry, `PATH`, removable in *Apps*).

**winget:** each release opens a pull request to
[winget-pkgs](https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs); `winget install hxddh.oprobe` works
only after Microsoft's review accepts the package. Until then (check with
`winget search hxddh.oprobe`), use one of the commands above or the `.msi`.

## Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora

```bash
sudo apt install ./oprobe_<ver>-1_amd64.deb
sudo dnf install ./oprobe-<ver>-1.x86_64.rpm
```

## From source

```bash
cargo install oprobe --locked                                         # the app in the terminal
cargo install oprobe --locked --features gui                          # plus native windows (Linux: libgtk-4-dev)
cargo install oprobe --locked --no-default-features --features cli    # the CLI only
cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/hxddh/oprobe --tag v6.0.0 oprobe
```

`cargo install oprobe` also downloads `oprobe-core`, oprobe's internal engine crate, at exactly
the same version. To embed oprobe's instrumentation in your own program use
[`oprobe-trace`](embedding.md).

## Verifying a download

The install scripts always check the SHA-256 and, when the GitHub CLI is installed and logged in,
the build provenance. A check that runs and fails stops the install; a check that cannot run is a
warning, or an error with `OPROBE_VERIFY=require`.

**Checksum.** Detects corrupted or truncated downloads. `SHA256SUMS` comes from the same release
as the archive, so it proves the download is intact, not who built it.

```bash
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS                    # Linux
shasum -a 256 --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS                # macOS
Get-FileHash oprobe-6.0.0-x64.msi -Algorithm SHA256          # Windows
```

**Build provenance.** Every asset has a [SLSA build provenance](https://slsa.dev/) attestation
signed by GitHub Actions, which proves it was built by this repository's release workflow from a
given commit:

```bash
gh attestation verify oprobe-6.0.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz --repo hxddh/oprobe \
  --signer-workflow hxddh/oprobe/.github/workflows/release.yml
```

**minisign.** The release workflow can also sign `SHA256SUMS` with minisign
(`SHA256SUMS.minisig`) and embed the public key in the install scripts, which then verify the
signature when `gh` is not available. This happens only for releases made with a signing key
configured; a release without `SHA256SUMS.minisig` is not signed, and its install scripts check
no signature. The release notes say which applies.

These say who built a file; they are not operating-system code signing (below).

## First open of unsigned packages

The project has no Apple or Microsoft code-signing certificate, so the `.pkg`, `.dmg` and `.msi`
are **not signed or notarized**. The operating system asks for one confirmation the first time:

- **macOS 15 (Sequoia) and later**: open `oprobe.app` (or the `.pkg`) once and close the warning;
  then open *System Settings → Privacy & Security*, scroll to the message about oprobe, click
  **Open Anyway** and confirm with your password.
- **macOS 14 and earlier**: right-click `oprobe.app` → *Open* → *Open*.
- **Either, from a terminal**: `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/oprobe.app`.
- **Windows**: SmartScreen says "Windows protected your PC": click **More info** → **Run anyway**.

Homebrew, Scoop, winget, the install scripts, `cargo install` and the plain archives used from a
terminal are not affected. Verify the download ([above](#verifying-a-download)) before you
confirm.


<!-- source: docs/troubleshooting.md -->

# Troubleshooting

`oprobe run` checks the operator before it measures (a preflight: credentials, the network path,
list and write permission on the prefix). When something is wrong it stops with an error that
carries a stable code (`-o json`: `error.code`, plus `error.docs` linking to this page) and usually
a `hint:` line. `--dry-run` shows the plan without sending a request.

## Common problems

| Code / symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `usage.unknown_target` | the `OPERATOR` is neither a URL, an `op.toml` file nor a configured name | pass a URL (`s3://bucket/prefix`), a file, or define `[operators.NAME]` in the config file |
| `usage.unknown_run` | no run matches the reference | `oprobe show --list`; use more characters of the id |
| `config.invalid`, `config.unknown_option` | a typo in `op.toml` or the config file, or an option the service does not know | the error names the key and the closest valid one ([op.toml](operator.md)) |
| `auth.no_credentials`, `auth.denied`, `AccessDenied`, `SignatureDoesNotMatch` | missing or wrong credentials | export `AWS_*` / `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` / `AZURE_STORAGE_*`, or set them in `[options]`; oprobe needs list/read/write/delete on the prefix, or measure read-only with `--existing PREFIX` |
| `net.tls`, `invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer` | a private CA or a TLS-inspecting proxy | `http.ca_cert = "corp.pem"` in `op.toml` (or `--set http.ca_cert=corp.pem`); `http.insecure = true` for development endpoints only |
| `net.dns`, `no addresses` | a wrong endpoint, or a network where only the proxy resolves names | check `options.endpoint`; set `HTTPS_PROXY` |
| `net.unreachable`, `connection refused` | nothing listening | check the endpoint and port; is MinIO or `oprobe lab` running? |
| `RequestTimeTooSkewed` | the local clock is off by more than 15 minutes | enable NTP |
| `PermanentRedirect`, `AuthorizationHeaderMalformed`, `region is missing` | wrong region | `--set options.region=…` or `AWS_REGION`; R2 uses `auto` |
| `safety.read_only` (exit 5) | a write under `--read-only` / `--existing` | drop the flag, or profile existing objects with `--existing PREFIX` |
| `safety.budget_exceeded` (exit 4) | a budget stopped the run | raise `--max-*`; the partial run is saved |
| exit 3 after `prove` | the change is worse on the objective | read the evidence; try another value with `--with` |

## Situations

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| leftover `oprobe-run-*` prefixes | a run was killed hard (a second Ctrl-C, OOM, power loss); delete the prefix with your usual tools |
| `client_bound` on a remote store | the profiling process is the bottleneck (CPU, tiny objects); the profile's `self` section says why. Larger objects or fewer workers |
| `oprobe` asks nothing in a script | it never prompts: pass an operator, and use `--non-interactive` to rule out redraws |
| `cannot open a window` | no display (SSH, a server): the app opens in the terminal; Linux packages built with `--features gui` need GTK 4 |
| `oprobe show FILE` fails on a file from `oprobe-trace` | the file is from a newer major version, or was cut short; write it again with `Handle::save` |
| macOS "cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified" / Windows SmartScreen | the packages are unsigned: [first open](install.md#first-open-of-unsigned-packages) |

## Error codes

Every error carries one of these codes. The exit code follows the class: `2` usage/config, `1`
runtime, `3` prove refuted, `4` budget, `5` safety refusal, `130` interrupted.

<a id="usage-invalid_argument"></a>
### `usage.invalid_argument` (exit 2)

A flag or argument is malformed: an unknown flag, a value that does not parse
(`--max-bytes lots`), an unknown `--set` path. With `-o json` argument errors are JSON too. Fix
the argument; `--help` lists what the command accepts.

<a id="usage-unknown_target"></a>
### `usage.unknown_target` (exit 2)

The `OPERATOR` is neither a URL, an existing `op.toml` file nor a name under `[operators.NAME]`
in the config file, or no operator was given. The hint lists the configured names.

<a id="usage-unknown_run"></a>
### `usage.unknown_run` (exit 2)

No stored run matches the reference. `oprobe show --list`; use more characters of the id,
`last`, `last~N`, a label, or a path to a `.oprobe` file.

<a id="usage-unknown_baseline"></a>
### `usage.unknown_baseline` (exit 2)

A 5.x baseline name was given. oprobe 6 has no baselines: compare runs in the app, or prove a
change with `oprobe prove`.

<a id="config-invalid"></a>
### `config.invalid` (exit 2)

An operator file or the config file does not parse, or has an invalid value (an unknown key, a
size that does not parse). The message names the key.

<a id="config-unknown_option"></a>
### `config.unknown_option` (exit 2)

A service option the OpenDAL service does not know (`[options]`, `--set options.KEY=…`). The
message names the closest valid option.

<a id="auth-no_credentials"></a>
### `auth.no_credentials` (exit 1)

No credentials were found. Export the provider's variables (`AWS_*`,
`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, `AZURE_STORAGE_*`) or set them in `[options]` (values may
reference `${ENV_VARS}`).

<a id="auth-denied"></a>
### `auth.denied` (exit 1)

The service refused the credentials or the operation (`AccessDenied`, `SignatureDoesNotMatch`,
403). oprobe needs list/read/write/delete on the prefix; profile read-only with
`--existing PREFIX`.

<a id="net-unreachable"></a>
### `net.unreachable` (exit 1, retryable)

Nothing answered (`connection refused`, reset, no route). Check the endpoint and port; is MinIO or
`oprobe lab` running? Behind an egress proxy check `HTTPS_PROXY` / `NO_PROXY`, or set
`http.proxy = "none"`.

<a id="net-dns"></a>
### `net.dns` (exit 1, retryable)

The endpoint's name did not resolve. Check `options.endpoint`; on networks where only the proxy
resolves names set `HTTPS_PROXY`.

<a id="net-tls"></a>
### `net.tls` (exit 1)

The TLS handshake failed (`invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer`, an expired or mismatched
certificate): a private CA or a TLS-inspecting proxy. Set `http.ca_cert` (or `SSL_CERT_FILE`);
`http.insecure = true` for development endpoints only.

<a id="net-timeout"></a>
### `net.timeout` (exit 1, retryable)

A request or connection timed out. Check the network path; lower the concurrency if the client or
the link is saturated. A timeout inside a run is a finding (`hung_requests`), not an error.

<a id="net-rate_limited"></a>
### `net.rate_limited` (exit 1, retryable)

An HTTP API other than the storage operator refused the request because its rate limit is
exhausted (429, or 403 with no quota left). Wait and retry. Your storage credentials are not
involved.

<a id="net-http"></a>
### `net.http` (exit 1)

An HTTP API other than the storage operator answered with an error. The message names the URL and
the status. Your storage credentials are not involved.

<a id="storage-not_found"></a>
### `storage.not_found` (exit 1)

The bucket, container, root or `--existing` prefix does not exist, or holds no objects. Check the
URL and region; with `--existing PREFIX` list the prefix first.

<a id="storage-throttled"></a>
### `storage.throttled` (exit 1, retryable)

The service rate-limited the preflight itself (429, 503 SlowDown). Inside a run, throttling is a
finding (`throttling`) and never fails the run: `oprobe prove RUN throttling` sizes the
`ConcurrentLimitLayer` that avoids it.

<a id="storage-unsupported"></a>
### `storage.unsupported` (exit 1)

The service does not support an operation the workload needs (multipart, list). Pick another
preset.

<a id="safety-budget_exceeded"></a>
### `safety.budget_exceeded` (exit 4)

A budget (`--max-requests`, `--max-bytes`, `--max-duration`, or `[defaults.budgets]`) stopped the
command. Budgets cover the whole command: every operator of `run`, every trial of `prove`. The
partial run is saved and test data cleaned up. Raise the budget or shorten the run; `--dry-run`
shows the estimates.

<a id="safety-read_only"></a>
### `safety.read_only` (exit 5)

The command would write or delete under `--read-only` / `--existing`. Drop the flag, or profile
existing objects with `--existing PREFIX`.

<a id="safety-refused"></a>
### `safety.refused` (exit 5)

A safety rail refused the command, for example deleting a run that is still being written, or a
lab limit.

<a id="run-sla_failed"></a>
### `run.sla_failed` (exit 3)

A 5.x SLA check failed. oprobe 6 reports failures as findings; exit 3 now means that `prove`
refuted the change.

<a id="run-regression"></a>
### `run.regression` (exit 3)

The change made things worse on the objective: `prove` refuted it. Read the evidence (the A/B
pairs and the secondary metrics); try another value with `--with`.

<a id="run-interrupted"></a>
### `run.interrupted` (exit 130, retryable)

Ctrl-C or Stop ended the command. Test data was cleaned up unless Ctrl-C was pressed twice. Run it
again.

<a id="internal"></a>
### `internal` (exit 1)

An unexpected failure. Rerun with the same arguments; if it persists, report it with the command
line and the error message.

[Reading the profile](reading-the-profile.md) explains each verdict and section.


<!-- source: docs/privacy.md -->

# Privacy

**oprobe sends no telemetry.** No usage statistics, crash reports or analytics, and no setting to
turn any on. Neither does `oprobe-trace`.

## What oprobe connects to

| When | Where |
|---|---|
| `run`, `prove`, the app | the storage endpoint of the operator you give it (and your proxy, if `HTTPS_PROXY` or `http.proxy` is set); that cloud's credential providers (instance metadata, STS, SSO) when the credential chain needs them |
| `demo`, `lab`, `lab://…` operators | nothing: the lab runs inside oprobe on 127.0.0.1 |
| `show`, `show --list`, `show --rm` | nothing |

Nothing else. oprobe never checks for updates by itself; the install scripts talk to GitHub when
you run them.

## What oprobe stores

- **Runs** in `<data dir>/oprobe/runs/` (or `$OPROBE_DATA_DIR`): the report, the operator spec,
  the workload and one row per operation and request. Object keys, request IDs and remote IP
  addresses are part of a run. Secrets are not: credential options (`secret_access_key`,
  `account_key`, `sas_token`, `password`, `*_key`, …) are redacted before anything is printed or
  saved, and URLs lose embedded credentials and query strings.
- **The host** is recorded as OS, architecture, CPU count and a hash of the host name, never the
  name itself.
- **The config file** holds what you put there.

Delete runs with `oprobe show --rm RUN…`, or remove the data directory.

## `.oprobe` files from `oprobe-trace`

`Handle::save` writes what the layer saw in your process: the aggregates and a sample of requests
with their API, method, status, timing, bytes, connection and request ID. Object keys are not part
of request rows, but request IDs and remote addresses are. Credentials never are. Review a file
before you attach it to an issue.

## Test data in your bucket

`oprobe run` writes under `<prefix>/oprobe-run-<id>/` and deletes it at the end, verifying the
prefix is empty. `--read-only` and `--existing` never write; `--dry-run` sends nothing. A run
killed hard (a second Ctrl-C, OOM, power loss) can leave its prefix behind; delete it with your
usual tools.
